confirmed.description: The flashback treatment is missing from the borders. The script asks for thin rounded panel borders on pages 5 and 6, but both pages use the same heavy square-cornered borders as the present-day pages, so nothing in the layout marks the jump to February.

It still matters less than the reviewer says, because the reader does not miss the time jump. The 5.1 caption says "February. Eight months before." The art switches from daytime laterite-hall interiors on page 4 to torchlit night on the beach at pages 5 and 6. The 7.1 caption brings the reader back with "Now, eight months later." The reviewer's line that "nothing in the layout marks the jump" is too strong. The caption and the day-to-night change both mark it. confirmed.description: The page grid is ragged. Panel 3.1 is shorter than 3.2 beside it, so the top row has misaligned top and bottom edges, and the 3.3 insert row is indented well inside the page margins. The page does not have the clean, aligned grid of the approved Chapter 1 pages.

confirmed.description: Ramayyan's long line, 'A Company doctor there lent us coin against Chanda Sahib...', sits on top of Nagoji, and its tail stops on Nagoji's sleeve. It crosses the tail of Nagoji's 'You trust him?', so readers will give Ramayyan's answer to Nagoji.

confirmed.description: The point of view is wrong. The script asks for Nagoji's distant look through Ibrahim's spyglass ('Through the glass, closer'), framed as a circular vignette like 21.2. The art is a full-colour shot from on board the ship, behind the officer on the quarterdeck, with no glass framing. The 'man seen from the ridge' beat becomes an omniscient shipboard view.
confirmed.evidence: Page 21, large middle panel: the camera is placed among the ship's own shrouds and rigging, looking at the officer's back at the stern rail, with a second ship behind him. There is no circular vignette, unlike 21.2 directly above.

verdict.reason: I confirmed the problem by cropping the panel at full resolution. Page 21, panel 21.3 (the large middle panel) is shot from on board the ship. The left foreground is filled with the ship's own shrouds, deadeyes and lanyards, and with its hull planking. The camera sits in the waist and looks up at the stern balustrade, the carved quarter gallery, a stern lantern and the ensign. A second Indiaman is visible behind. The panel has no circular vignette, no dark spyglass surround and no sense of distance. The script asks for the opposite: "Through the glass, closer ... Distant. No clear features." It follows 21.2, which is a vignette, and 21.4 has Nagoji "lowering the glass". As drawn, the beat stops being the man Nagoji sees from the ridge and becomes an all-seeing shipboard shot. That breaks the first-person narration ("I had seen that stillness") and the setup from 21.1 ("where their glass could find me"). Because 21.2, directly above, uses the vignette, the inconsistency is plain at print size. This is not a blocker: the content the beat needs is still there. The officer is tall, in a Dutch blue coat with gold trim, hands clasped behind his back, black tricorne, pale hair at the collar, and his face is hidden. The fix is local to this one panel: redraw it as a circular glass view from shore, or frame it that way. Small extra point: his feet look close together rather than "planted apart against the roll".

confirmed.description: The script's flashback treatment for pages 5 and 6 (a warmer, slightly faded palette and thin rounded panel borders) is not applied. The borders are the same heavy square black frames as the present-day pages, and the palette is fully saturated. Only the caption tells the reader this is a flashback.
confirmed.evidence: A zoom on the page 5 panel corners shows square corners and the same thick black border as page 3. Page 6 panels have the same square borders and saturated night colours.

verdict.reason: Confirmed. Script line 149 (CHAPTER-11-SCRIPT.md, Page 5) asks for a flashback treatment on pages 5 and 6: "a warmer, slightly faded palette and thin rounded panel borders". Page 6 says the treatment continues. Nothing in CONTINUITY.md, the adaptation notes or the author-decision memory removes it, and chapters 13, 14, 17 and 21 use their own flashback treatments, so this is a book-wide convention. What the renders show: (1) Borders. I zoomed 8x on the top-left corner of p5 panel 1, the bottom-right of p5 panel 2, the top-left of p6 panel 1 and a corner of p6 panel 3, and compared them with p3 panel 1. Every corner is square, and the black frame looks the same thickness as on present-day page 3. None of the borders on pages 5 and 6 is rounded or differently weighted. (2) Palette. I measured mean HSV saturation over the same interior panel area on each page: p5 105, p6 104, compared with p3 79, p4 84, p7 91 and p8 74. The red-minus-blue warmth offset is about the same on every page (p5 40, p6 39, p3 43, p4 41). The 2nd-percentile luminance is 0 on all pages, so the blacks are not lifted. The flashback pages are therefore more saturated than the present day, not faded, and no warmer. The image prompts did ask for "a warmer, slightly faded flashback palette", but the images do not carry it out. At print size the reader can tell this is a flashback only from the "February. Eight months before." caption and the switch from day to night. The treatment the script asks for is missing. It is localized to two pages, and the border fix belongs in compositing, so it does not need a full redraw. Because the night setting and the caption still carry the time shift, this is not a blocker. Severity: major.

confirmed.description: The gold-chain chief's locked design is not kept. On 12.2 and 12.3 he is fleshy and balding, with sparse curly side hair. The man who speaks 'The company pays fair weight' on 13.2, and the chief in the 13.1 inset, has a full head of black hair in a bun with a gold pin and a red-and-gold shoulder cloth. He reads as a different chief.
confirmed.evidence: Page 12, middle panel: the centre chief is bald on top with heavy chains. Page 13, bottom panel: the speaker, seen from behind, has a thick black bun with a gold hairpin. The page 13 top inset shows the same bun-haired man glancing back at Ibrahim.

verdict.reason: Confirmed after zooming in. Script 12.2 says the three chiefs' "designs [are] locked for this chapter". On page 12, panels 12.2 and 12.3, the gold-chain chief is fleshy, bald on top, has sparse curly hair at the sides and a heavy moustache, wears several heavy gold chains with pendants, and has rings and a red-striped shoulder cloth. On page 13 the same chief looks like a different man. In the 13.1 main panel (back of head, right) and in the 13.1 inset (glance toward Ibrahim), he has a full head of thick black hair in a bun with a curved gold pin, gold stud earrings and a red-and-gold brocade shoulder cloth. In 13.2 the speaker of "The company pays fair weight" also has a thick black bun with a gold-beaded pin and gold hoop earrings. He wears strands of round gold beads rather than heavy chains with pendants, a large red-and-gold brocade shoulder cloth, and his back is muscular, not fleshy. The change from bald to a full bun is an identity change that is easy to see at print size, not slight. It also weakens the plant: the 12.2 caption ties debt to the bald chief, and 13.1 links Ibrahim to that same chief. Neither the bible nor the cast overrides allow the change; neither has a 13.1 or 13.2 entry. I rate it major rather than blocker. The dialogue still works, the speaker still wears gold, the character appears only in this chapter, and the fix stays on one page: redraw the 13.1 back-of-head figure and inset and the 13.2 foreground chief as the bald, fleshy man from 12.2 with heavy chains.

confirmed.description: The chief in white is not the man from 12.2. On 12.2 he is lean and older, with grey swept-back hair and a lined face. On 14.1 he is a smooth-faced younger man with slicked black hair, and on 14.5 he has curly black hair. The Kottarakkara question therefore comes from someone the reader has not met.
confirmed.evidence: Page 12, middle panel, right: grey-haired older man in white. Page 14, top panel: young clean-faced man with black hair. Page 14, bottom-right panel: curly black-haired man lowering his eyes.

verdict.reason: I zoomed in on all three panels and the problem is real. On 12.2 (right figure), the chief in white is an older man. He has grey-streaked hair receding at the temples, deep forehead and cheek lines, and a gaunt face. On 14.1 (the big top panel), he is clearly a younger man in his thirties, with a smooth unlined face and thick, glossy, all-black slicked-back hair. On 14.5 (bottom right, eyes lowered), he has thick, wavy black hair and yet another face shape, with no grey and no lines. The script (12.2) says the designs of the three chiefs are "locked for this chapter". Page 14's notes describe him as "lean, upright, no ornaments", so the 12.2 look is the reference. CONTINUITY.md and the cast overrides have no entry that would allow a different look. The only links back to 12.2 are the plain white mundu, the shoulder cloth and the lack of ornaments. That is not enough, because 14.1 is a full-width close-up where the age and hair change is obvious at print size. Readers will take the man asking "What of Kottarakkara?" for someone new, and that weakens the chapter's key beat. This is a wrong-identity error on a minor, chapter-only character, confined to two panels, so I rate it major rather than blocker. 14.1 and 14.5 should be redrawn to match the older, grey-haired chief from 12.2.

confirmed.description: Revathi wears a dot mark between her brows. The script says she is a widow and 'the sandalwood line at her hairline is her only forehead mark.' The parting of her hair is also tinted orange on several panels (9.5, 11.2, 18.3), which can read as sindoor.
confirmed.evidence: Zoomed crops show a small dark-red vertical mark between the brows on 18.3 (Revathi beside Nagoji at the pillar), and a dark dot on 17.5 (split tier, left) and 19.1. An orange streak runs along the hair parting on 11.2 and 18.3.

verdict.reason: The claim holds. I zoomed in on each panel. 18.3: Revathi has a dark red vertical mark between her brows, below the sandalwood line, and an orange-red streak runs down her hair parting. The brow mark is visible at full-page size. 19.1: a clear dark dot between her brows, also visible on the unzoomed page. 17.5 (left tier): a dark dot between her brows. 11.2: an orange streak runs along the parting above the sandalwood line. 18.5 shows the same orange tint in the parting but no dot. 19.3 is clean. The script rules this out in two places. 8.1 says she is a widow with "no tali, no sindoor in the parting; the sandalwood line at her hairline is her only forehead mark", and 9.5 repeats it. The notes add "Revathi is still a widow: no tali, no sindoor." CONTINUITY.md gives her the sandalwood line only, with no dot. The likely source is the approved sheet, 05-revathi-bayi-v15f.png, which has a tiny dark dot between the brows and a faint orange tint at the parting. That makes it a known sheet fault that needs a prompt caveat, not something the bible allows. At print size, the red mark on 18.3 together with the tinted parting reads as a married woman's markings on a character the script makes a widow, so it changes what the reader understands about her. It is localized, though: three faces need the dot retouched and three or four partings need the tint removed (11.2, 18.3, 18.5). Nothing needs a full redraw, so major, not blocker. Separate from this claim: 11.2 also has an extra, empty speech balloon at top right with a tail pointing into the art, which is a lettering defect.

confirmed.description: The staging breaks the pillar conversation. On 18.3 to 18.5 Revathi stands beside Nagoji at his pillar. On 19.1 and 19.3 she is suddenly seated on the floor in the crowd, and the betel-box chief she mocks sits right next to her instead of 'across the hall in a different cluster'. Her aside about his debt now plays as if said within his earshot.
confirmed.evidence: Page 19, top panel: Revathi sits on the mat about a metre from the grey-haired chief with the brass betel box, with no pillar or Nagoji present. Page 19, middle-right panel: she is seated among the Velinadu women. Page 18, middle panel: she was standing at the pillar.

verdict.reason: Confirmed on zoomed crops of page 19. On 19.1 Revathi sits cross-legged on the mat inside the betel-box chief's own circle. She is within arm's reach of him, with seated men in the foreground on both sides. There is no pillar and no Nagoji in the panel. She gives the chief a side-glance while he talks, so her two lines about his Dutch debt read as said within his earshot. The script asks for something else on 19.1: "a chief across the hall, seated in a different cluster", and 18.3 sets her standing beside Nagoji at his pillar. On 19.3 she is seated on the mat again, with Velinadu women behind her, and again no pillar and no Nagoji. On 19.2, between those panels, Nagoji is still standing at his pillar. So the private aside of 18.3 to 19.3 (spoken in Konkani so that few could follow) is broken in space across two panels. Nothing in the script, the cast overrides or the bible allows a seated or close-up staging. The cast list for 19.1 is just Revathi, but the script text clearly puts the chief across the hall. The problem is easy to see at print size. Severity is major, not blocker: identities, costumes, lettering and the dialogue beat are all intact. The error is limited to how 19.1 and 19.3 are staged, and both should be redrawn with Revathi standing at the pillar, with the chief small and distant in 19.1.

confirmed.description: 'And our sand' is not given room. The script says 'Give the answer room', with 17.2 'Tighter. His eyes.' Both panels are thin strips at the top of the page, and 17.2 is framed almost the same as 17.1 (turban to chest), so the key line of the court scene does not build to the eye close-up.
confirmed.evidence: Page 17, top tier: two short strips (about 180px tall at display size). The 17.2 shot is only slightly tighter than 17.1 and shows the full turban and moustache, not an eye close-up.

verdict.reason: This is partly confirmed, but it is minor, not major. On page 17 the top tier is about 253 px tall in the 1838x2775 render at 300 DPI, roughly 0.84 in at print. Panels 17.1 and 17.2 sit side by side in that one strip, the thinnest tier on the page. Panel 17.2 is not the eye close-up the script asks for ("Tighter. His eyes."). It is a head-and-shoulders shot with the turban, moustache, pearl earring and bead necklaces all in frame. The reviewer overstates one point: 17.2 is clearly tighter than 17.1, not "almost the same." Varma's head is about 1.4 to 1.6 times larger, the top of the turban is cut off, and his frowning eyes are easy to read. Nothing is missing. Both lines are lettered and readable, each in its own panel with the tail on the speaker, and the push-in works as a staccato build. The big memory-flicker panel 17.3 then gives "And our sand" its room as a payoff. The script's page note supports that reading. Wrong identity, illegible lettering or a lost beat would make this major or a blocker, and none of those is here. A taller top tier with an eye close-up in 17.2 would be better, which makes this a polish note.

refuted.description: The bible-required brand beat is missing. The drawn hand is Nagoji's RIGHT hand, seen palm down with the back of the hand and the outer forearm to camera. Neither the edge of the brand nor the ridged nails are visible. CONTINUITY 11 @24.3 calls for the LEFT palm on the rock, the forearm turned so the edge of the pale puckered brand shows on the INNER left forearm a hand's width above the wrist, and ridged nails.
refuted.reason: I zoomed in on page 24, panel 3, and the art does not show the reported problem. 1) It is the LEFT hand. We see the back of the hand, with the nails showing and the fingertips pointing down toward the reader. The thumb is on the image-left side. For the back of a hand with the fingers pointing down, that combination is a left hand, not a right one. The body agrees: Nagoji's head is turned in profile toward image-left, which puts his LEFT side toward the camera, so the arm reaching down to the near rock is his left arm. The reviewer had both rules of thumb backwards. 2) The edge of the brand is there. On the image-left edge of the bare forearm (the thumb side, where the inner forearm rolls into view), about 50 to 220 px above the wrist crease at 300 DPI, which is roughly a hand's width, there is a pale, glossy, hairless strip with small raised beads. It is clearly different from the hairy skin around it. That matches the bible's 11 @24.3 note: only the edge of the brand shows, on the inner forearm, never on the back of the hand. The script's 24.3 note, 'just visible', also fits. The sleeve is pushed back as the bible asks, and the long white scar is covered, as allowed. 3) Ridged nails: the nails show faint lengthwise striations at high zoom, but ridging is too small to read at print size whatever is drawn. That is polish at most, not a missing beat. The panel follows the continuity bible and the script.

refuted.description: De Lannoy's hair is wrong for his sheet. Below the tricorne it is drawn as grey-white curls at the nape, which reads as an elderly officer or a powdered wig. Together with the gold-braided navy coat, the figure echoes Van Imhoff's powdered-wig look from pages 5 and 6, so readers may take the man on the quarterdeck for the governor.

(4) The parting line is not sindoor. In 9.5, 11.2, 18.3 and 18.5 it scans as an amber or ochre scalp highlight: hue 26 to 34 degrees, for example (150,67,0) in 9.5 and (230,138,50) in 11.2. He is the large foreground figure caught in the act of bowing toward Varma. The interpreter faces the viewer, mouth closed and hands clasped, a passive bystander. Even if a reader does give the line to the interpreter, no beat or identity is lost. The script places the interpreter "at his elbow" and has him translating on the next page (9.1, "blinking before he translates"), and page 9 panel 1 itself routes an ENVOY line through the interpreter. So the Company's greeting coming out of the interpreter's mouth makes sense in the story. Optional polish: shorten the tail or move its tip about 30 px left, onto the envoy's forehead, to remove any doubt. This is not a major problem.

refuted.reason: The measurements are right, but the problem doesn't hold up. In the full-resolution crop of page 17's bottom tier, the gutter sits at about x918. Revathi's balloon runs from about x615 to x1040. Ramayyan's balloon runs from about x635 to x1255, so roughly 46% of it lies on Revathi's side. The script says otherwise: CHAPTER-11-SCRIPT.md line 745 gives the reason as "17.5: split tier so Revathi and Ramayyan keep their seats." The split is about where they sit. Line 469 asks only for two side-by-side panels, and I found no rule in CONTINUITY.md or the script that keeps balloons from crossing a gutter. The lettering itself works. Revathi's balloon is top-left, so it reads first, and its tail points left to her mouth. Ramayyan's balloon sits below it and its wedge tail points right at his face, so the speakers and reading order are clear. Neither balloon covers a face or key action: Revathi's face, Ramayyan's face, and his stylus and palm leaf are all clear. The overlap only covers background women and the gutter. Balloons bridging a split tier are normal lettering practice and hard to misread at print size. At most this is a matter of taste, not a major error.

Comics readers follow a tail's direction, and this one points at the envoy, as the script requires for both ENVOY lines. Both balloons read left to right, and both tails angle toward the envoy, so the two lines read as his. The only weakness is that the balloon sits under the interpreter and the tail stops short of the envoy. That leaves slight ambiguity, which is optional polish: lengthen the tail toward the envoy's mouth, or join the two balloons with a connector. It is not a wrong speaker tail and does not warrant a major finding.

So the reviewer's statement that the forearm skin is unmarked is wrong; the brand edge is drawn where the bible puts it, and it is meant to be quiet. His horse is not shown standing toward the camera either. The breastplate and chest point to frame-left and the tail hangs toward Nagoji at frame-right, so the horse is turned away from Nagoji. He is drawn about half Ibrahim's scale, higher in the frame and set against the sunset sea, so he reads as left behind against the copper sea as scripted. minors.evidence: Pages 10.2, 11.2, 12.1 and 12.2 have pink and violet dusk skies. Page 14.1 and 15.1 show high noon with blue sky. Page 18.1 is golden afternoon.

minors.description: The script calls for a strip of three small insets. The panel adds a fourth, establishing image above them (Padmini, Revathi and the envoys), and its top edge sits lower than 18.1.
minors.evidence: Page 18, top-right panel: a wide image of Padmini, Revathi and the envoys sits above the three insets, starting about 45px below the top of 18.1.

minors.description: The script asks for a wide shot with the riders deliberately in silhouette and Nagoji's profile edge-lit. It is a half-width panel, the riders are seen from behind and fully lit, and the caption covers the horses.
minors.evidence: Page 21, top-left panel: Ibrahim and Nagoji are lit from the front and seen from the back. The caption box sits over the lower centre.

minors.description: Ibrahim's scar from the LEFT ear to the jaw should be clear in the low light. It is barely visible, and the balloon tail ends right on it.

minors.description: The haze smudging one cluster of ship lights is barely visible, and three caption boxes cover most of the panel. The 'Ship smoke. Dutch smoke.' caption is not set apart or weighted as the script asks.
minors.evidence: Page 24, bottom-left panel: the light clusters at the horizon are tiny and show no clear smudge. The three caption boxes are the same size and style.

minors.description: The script asks for the chapter's closing pull-back to be full width, with four clusters of light. It is a half-width panel beside 24.4, and only three light clusters are visible.
minors.evidence: Page 24, bottom-right panel: half the page width, with a tiny figure on the bluff and three clusters of light on the water.

minors.description: Revathi is seated at the very front beside Padmini and next to Nagoji's pillar. The script places her farther back among the older Velinadu women, and 17.5 refers back to her as 'far back'.
minors.evidence: Page 8, top panel: Revathi in the green sari sits directly behind Padmini at the front, beside Nagoji.
